title: Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
meta_title: Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
meta_description: Paracetamol for arthritis: what NICE says about osteoarthritis, the limits of trial evidence, medicine checks and when to seek urgent help. UK adult guide.
excerpt: Paracetamol is not a routine osteoarthritis treatment under NICE guidance. Understand the evidence, avoid doubling up on medicines, and prepare a safer medicines review.

content:
Quick answer: Paracetamol has little average benefit for hip or knee osteoarthritis. NICE says not to offer it routinely for osteoarthritis, except for infrequent, short-term relief when other drug treatments cannot be used, are not tolerated or have not worked. A personal medicines review matters more than increasing the dose. Do not change prescribed treatment solely because of this page.

This guide is for adults in the UK. It separates evidence about osteoarthritis from advice for inflammatory arthritis, and explains what to check before taking another dose. It cannot tell you which medicine or dose is safe for your own health conditions.

What does the evidence actually show?

A 2019 Cochrane review included 10 trials with 3,541 people who had hip or knee osteoarthritis. Most studies lasted three months or less. Compared with placebo, paracetamol improved pain by about 3 points on a 100-point scale on average, below the review's threshold for an important improvement. Physical-function benefits were similarly small.

These are average results, not proof that every individual experiences exactly the same effect. They also do not establish long-term safety: overall adverse events were similar to placebo, but there were too few serious events to be certain about serious side effects and the clinical importance of liver-test changes. The review searched for trials up to October 2017. It is an evidence summary, not a new 2026 trial or a reason to describe paracetamol as harmless.

What does current NICE guidance recommend?

NICE guideline NG226, recommendation 1.4.5 says not to routinely offer paracetamol for osteoarthritis. Its exception has both conditions: use is infrequent and short term, and all other drug treatments are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. NICE explains that there is no strong evidence of benefit. This is more specific than saying it is the standard first choice for any mild arthritis pain.

For osteoarthritis, therapeutic exercise and information remain central. NICE recommends a topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), such as a suitable gel, for knee osteoarthritis, and says to consider one for other affected joints. Oral NSAIDs are an option when topical medicines are unsuitable or ineffective, but need checks for stomach, kidney, liver and cardiovascular risks and other medicines. NICE recommends offering stomach protection, such as a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), while taking an oral NSAID for osteoarthritis. This does not remove all NSAID risks. Do not switch yourself to ibuprofen or another NSAID on the strength of this comparison. Ask a pharmacist or clinician what fits your situation.

Does this apply to rheumatoid arthritis too?

Not in the same way. The trials above concerned hip or knee osteoarthritis, not every cause of joint pain. The NHS rheumatoid arthritis treatment page describes paracetamol as an option that may sometimes be advised for pain alongside other treatment. Painkillers do not replace medicines used to control the disease and reduce joint damage.

If pain, stiffness or swelling is increasing despite your plan, contact your rheumatology team or GP for a review rather than just adding painkillers. Do not stop or change a disease-modifying medicine to make room for paracetamol or a supplement. Our medicines and supplements guide explains what information to bring to that conversation.

Check the packet, strength and total across products

The NHS adult paracetamol guidance says to follow the packet or leaflet. For standard 500 mg adult tablets or capsules, it describes one or two per dose, at least four hours between doses, and no more than eight in 24 hours. This is a maximum for that product and standard adult guidance, not a target or a personalised prescription. A 1 g tablet already contains twice as much as a 500 mg tablet. NHS guidance for 1 g tablets is only one at a time and no more than four in 24 hours; a lower individual limit may apply. Liquids have different concentrations, so tablet counts do not apply to them.

If you weigh less than 50 kg, you may need a lower dose. Check with a pharmacist or doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, alcohol dependence or binge drinking, a previous allergy to paracetamol, or uncertainty about suitability. Follow an individual lower-dose plan if one has been given to you. NHS advice is not to use paracetamol for more than three days unless a doctor tells you to; an existing prescribed plan should be discussed with the prescriber, not replaced by this article.

Do not accidentally double up

Cold and flu remedies and combination painkillers may already contain paracetamol. Co-codamol contains paracetamol: do not add separate paracetamol or another paracetamol-containing product unless a doctor has advised it. Check ingredients rather than relying on different brand names.

Show a pharmacist your full list of prescriptions, bought medicines and supplements. NHS guidance flags potential problems with medicines including warfarin and flucloxacillin. A short list in an article cannot clear all combinations as safe. Do not take an extra dose because the first one has not helped.

When to get help rather than wait

If you may have taken too much

Get urgent medical advice now if you have taken more paracetamol than the packet or leaflet says. Call NHS 111 in England, Scotland or Wales. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service for urgent advice. Do not wait for symptoms or assume you are safe because you feel well. Liver UK explains that urgent assessment matters even before symptoms appear. Have the packets, amounts and times ready, including combination medicines. Follow the urgent service's instructions about attending hospital.

If a joint suddenly becomes very painful or swollen

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact the urgent-care service above for sudden severe joint pain, swelling, skin colour changes, difficulty moving a joint, or joint pain with fever or feeling unwell. NHS septic arthritis advice says these symptoms need checking straight away; not everyone has a fever. Do not wait a week or use pain relief to postpone assessment.

Call 999 in an immediate emergency, such as severe breathing difficulty, sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, collapse or inability to wake someone. Do not use routine medicines advice to delay emergency care.

A useful medicines review: three questions

  1. What is this medicine helping me do? Note whether it changes sleep, walking, dressing or another activity that matters to you, not only a pain score.
  2. What is my safe plan? Confirm the product, dose limit, spacing, duration and what to do if it does not help, taking your other conditions and medicines into account.
  3. What should happen next? Agree when to review treatment and who to contact if pain or swelling increases. Bring your packets and a short symptom and flare record rather than trying to remember every dose.

For osteoarthritis, use the osteoarthritis guide to prepare questions about exercise and other treatment options. The aim is a workable, reviewed plan, not the largest allowable amount of medicine.

About this revision

The latest check clarified stomach protection with oral NSAIDs and urgent-care routes across the UK. It has not yet had a fresh clinical review and is awaiting a separate qualified clinical review.
